definition: Real assets are properties whose value comes from their physical substance or attributes (tangible), though a small subset — such as patents, trademarks, and artwork — have value without physical form (intangible).
core_idea: In energy markets, real assets are mostly tangible (oil, land, drilling equipment, refineries, power lines, generation facilities) and trade in spot markets in a limited, largely one-directional way because storing and transporting them is complex.
key_points: Tangible real assets in energy: oil, land, drilling equipment, refineries, power lines, power generation facilities.
Intangible real assets are less common in energy markets: examples given are patents, advertising trademarks, and works of art.
Real asset transactions tend to be one-directional — a buyer purchases to use the asset, not to resell it.
Most commodity trading activity actually happens in derivatives markets rather than the physical (real asset) spot market.
relationships: Contrasted with financial assets, which are created by issuers rather than existing as physical/tangible property.
Real assets serve as the underlying asset for most energy derivatives (e.g., crude oil, electricity).
trading_implications: Because physical storage/transport is complex, liquidity and active trading concentrate in derivatives on real assets rather than the real assets themselves.
